1:
The name is where three commentators begin. Gill takes it for a habitation for God to dwell in, which is what the word properly signifies, and reads it as a type twice over — of the human nature of Christ, the true tabernacle God pitched and not man, and of the church, where he grants his presence and accepts the sacrifices of prayer and praise. Ellicott renders it literally as the dwelling, from the verb translated dwell just before. Clarke traces the same root and turns it into a picture: it means a dwelling place of any kind, but here Jehovah's, who like a king in his camp had his pavilion among his people, his table always spread, his lamps lighted, and the priests his attendants in waiting.

Henry reads the choice of a tent rather than a house as deliberate on two counts. It suited their condition, so that they might have God with them wherever they went — God suits the tokens of his favour to his people's necessities, settled or unsettled. And it represented the church's state in this world, a tabernacle-state: we have no continuing city here, and shall never be fixed until heaven. He presses that further than comfort: church privileges are movable goods, the gospel is tied to no place, and a candlestick standing in a tent may as easily be taken away.

On the workmanship the notes are precise. Clarke distinguishes the two terms used in this chapter — the first probably a sort of diaper in which the figures show equally perfect on both sides, formed in the loom, the second the needlework of the door hanging. Ellicott draws the same contrast more exactly, the one signifying work where the patterning was inwoven and the other where it was embroidered, and notes that inweaving figures was well understood in Egypt; the fine twined linen, he adds, means thread made by twisting several strands together, as Egyptian thread ordinarily was. Clarke reckons that from a description this minute a good workman with the same materials could produce a facsimile, and wonders where such work was done. It seems unlikely to him that all of it was made in the wilderness: what came off a loom they may have brought from Egypt, and what a hand could do the women could manage with their needles — though he thinks they probably brought the looms too, and concludes that the ornamental arts as well as the necessary had reached a considerable pitch among both peoples.

The embroidered cherubim draw one reading from Henry and Wesley alike: the angels of God pitch their tents round about the church, and as there were cherubim over the mercy seat, so there were round the tabernacle. Both read the coupling of the two great hangings the same way, that the churches of Christ, though many, are one, fitly joined by holy love and the unity of the Spirit — and both notice how small the enclosure was, against the later summons to enlarge the place of her tent.

Calvin agrees the richness has a lesson in it, since all this magnificence was the contrast to meanness and taught how precious a thing the worship of God is; the outward ornament, on his reading, designated the excellency of spiritual gifts. But he sets a limit against the method before the chapter is fairly begun. Readers should expect no conceits to gratify their ears: it was by no means God's intention to include mysteries in every hook and loop, and even if no part were without a mystical meaning — which no one in his senses will admit — it is better to confess ignorance than indulge conjecture. The writer to the Hebrews he takes for a model of that restraint, touching sparingly on the main points and by his moderation holding readers back from deep speculation.
2:
The measurements are given once and then held to. Keil and Delitzsch set out each breadth at twenty-eight cubits by four, all of one measure, five of them sewn into a piece twenty-eight cubits long and twenty broad, and the other five into its fellow. Ellicott adds a reason for the arithmetic that the text does not give. Fergusson has shown that to roof a space twenty cubits wide with two sides meeting at a right angle, a tent-cloth of almost exactly twenty-eight cubits would be wanted — so the length is not arbitrary but follows from the pitch of the roof.

Why two curtains rather than one is answered practically. Ellicott takes the object to have been portability: a single covering of that size would have been too heavy and too bulky to carry conveniently. He also flags a small grammatical oddity, that the definite article in the clause about the five curtains is anomalous and has probably crept in from the preceding verse; the sense required is that five breadths be sewn to form one curtain and five more to form another, the two then joined by loops and clasps.

Over the loops both he and Keil and Delitzsch are careful about the mechanism. Fifty loops of blue were to be set along the extreme edge of each half, at the point where the two would meet — Ellicott would read the phrase as at the coupling rather than from the selvedge — and the loops in one half were to answer exactly to the loops in the other. Ellicott corrects the English here as well: they were not to take hold of each other but to correspond, being fastened by golden links, which he supposes may have been split-rings or something like modern sleeve-links. Gill canvasses what the fastenings were called, buttons by some and hooks by others, and settles on clasps.

The closing clause is where Ellicott finds the point of the whole arrangement. He would render it and so the tabernacle shall be one, and reads it as guarding against a consequence of the design: dividing the roof-curtain in two tended to divide the tabernacle itself, and the looping was ordered precisely so that the two should be practically one and the dwelling remain undivided. Keil and Delitzsch draw a further inference from the same clasps. Because the two halves answered to the two compartments within, they follow Bähr in concluding that the cloth enclosed the whole interior — hanging down the side walls on the outside of the wooden framework rather than being stretched over it as a ceiling, so that the gilded beams were left visible from inside.
7:
The second covering is coarser and the commentators say why. Gill describes the material as the flower or down of goats, the softer and finer part of the hair, spun by women into a stuff something like camlet, and reckons these curtains coarser than the first and laid over them to keep off the weather. Keil and Delitzsch note that the tents of the Bedouin are still made of cloth woven from black goats' hair, spun and woven by the women. Ellicott corrects the English word: literally it is a tent, not a covering, and the eleven curtains are eleven breadths.

The arithmetic of the eleventh breadth is the interesting part. Keil and Delitzsch have five pieces sewn together and six, with the sixth folded double toward the front so as to form a kind of gable, as Josephus describes. Ellicott says the same more plainly, that the additional breadth was doubled back on itself to give the roof a sort of finish at the front. What was left over went to the other end: even after the doubling the goats'-hair covering was still half a breadth wider than the linen one, and that half-breadth was to hang down at the back. Gill and Keil both account for the extra length the same way — the goats'-hair curtains were two cubits longer, a cubit falling on each side, and it hung over the sides of the dwelling to cover them.

Two more coverings go over that, and here nobody is sure of the material. Clarke counts them as the third and fourth, and admits that why there should have been four coverings does not appear; his guesses are partly respect, partly the fine sand of the desert that rises on every breeze, and partly the intense heat, which would otherwise have destroyed the poles, bars, boards and all the woodwork. Wesley will not defend the usual rendering of the outermost: it should rather seem to have been some strong but very fine leather, since the best sort of shoes are said to be made of it. Gill leaves open whether the rams' skins covered the whole or only the roof, reporting Jarchi for the roof alone but thinking it more reasonable that the whole was covered to keep off dust and rain. Ellicott argues the point from function: since the object of the two outer coverings must have been to keep out rain, they cannot have protected the ridge only but must have covered the whole dwelling, which fixes their length at thirty cubits and their breadth at fourteen.

Henry reads the same layers for their moral rather than their measurements, and he is careful about which way it runs. The outside of the tabernacle was coarse and rough and the beauty was in the inner curtains: those in whom God dwells must labour to be better than they seem, where hypocrites put the best side outward, like whited sepulchres. The church is in the world's eye black as the tents of Kedar and in God's comely as the curtains of Solomon, the king's daughter being all glorious within. He notices too that the clasps of this covering were brass where the inner ones were gold, the stuff being less valuable — and that the brass answered the intention as effectually, since the bonds of unity may be as strong between curtains of goats' hair as between purple and scarlet. His second point is about protection rather than modesty: where God places his glory he will create a defence upon it, and the tent that houses it becomes a pavilion.
15:
What the boards were for is stated before what they were like. Gill calls them the pillars and supports and properly the walls, which gave the structure its firmness — without them the curtains would have been blown about by every wind. Henry says the same and turns it into the figure he wants: it is a good thing to have the heart established with grace, which is as the boards supporting the curtains of a profession that will not otherwise hold out long.

The dimensions are agreed and the thickness is not. Keil and Delitzsch give each board as ten cubits by a cubit and a half, standing upright, and observe that the text says nothing about how thick they were. They decline both extremes: not so thin as Josephus, who makes them four fingers, but still less a cubit thick, as Rashi and others would have it, since that turns simple boards into colossal blocks that could neither be cut from acacia trees nor carried along desert roads. Clarke converts the measurements into yards and infers the height of the whole from them, the boards standing up; Ellicott simply refers the question of whether boards fifteen feet long could be got from the acacia back to his earlier note.

Clarke raises a practical difficulty nobody else does. To work acacia into planks the Israelites must have had sawyers and joiners among them — but where did the tools come from? His answer is that as the general workmen of Egypt they had been brought up to every trade for their oppressors' service, so that each artificer probably carried off the implements of his own craft; they had no armour or weapons, but the tools of a trade are another matter.

The joinery is described exactly. Keil and Delitzsch render the projections as hands or holders, pegs to keep each board upright, and argue that the boards were not pegged into one another but joined by a fastening dovetailed into the pegs, which held far better than a peg sunk into the edge of a board. Ellicott does the arithmetic that follows from it: twenty boards with two tenons apiece require exactly forty sockets. Gill describes those sockets as properly the foundation of the whole, mortises as broad as the plank, joining each other so as to make one entire base for the structure, and reckons each at a talent of silver from the offering taken at the numbering of the people.

Henry looks at the finished thing and reads the splendour historically rather than symbolically. Everything in the tabernacle was made strong as well as fine, and everything was made rich — which he takes as suited to the infant state of the church, when such things were proper to fill worshippers with reverence for the divine glory and to impress them with the greatness of the prince who said he would dwell there. Wesley repeats the point almost word for word. Henry then sets against it the contrast he is really after: the builders of the gospel church said silver and gold have they none, and the glory of their building far exceeded this. He also notices what the chapter omits — no orders are given about the floor. He supposes it was boarded too, since we cannot think that within all these fine curtains they trod on cold or wet ground; but if it was left bare, he says, that has its own echo in the command for an altar of earth.
22:
The rear of the structure is where the description goes obscure, and Ellicott begins by correcting the compass. What the English calls the sides westward is rather the back of the tabernacle, since Orientals always reckon the west as behind; the Greek renders it so. Gill takes the same clause as meaning the ends, east and west, and notes that the account begins with the west.

Then the arithmetic fails to close, and Ellicott says so plainly. Six boards of the standard width come to nine cubits only, where ten are wanted — so the tenth cubit must have been made up by the corner boards, which are counted along with the six as forming the back. Gill goes to Lightfoot for a fuller reconstruction: the west end had six planks entire besides a plank at either corner joining end and sides together, these corner planks being of the same breadth as all the rest, and set so that the middle of the breadth of the one lay close against the end of the south side. How they were held is described without being explained. Keil and Delitzsch record only that they were coupled below and above, at the head, into one ring, with sixteen sockets under the eight boards of the back; Ellicott supplies the mechanism he thinks is meant, a single ring in each of the two places, and takes those rings to be the ones through which the ends of the bars afterwards passed.

The bars are the last of the framing, and their purpose is stated more clearly than their arrangement. Gill has them put into rings or staples of gold to keep the boards tight and close and firm together; Ellicott makes the object to be preventing any aperture between one board and another, counts fifteen in all, five to each of the three boarded sides, and distinguishes the middle bar — it ran the whole length of the side, where the four above and below were shorter and each probably coupled half the boards of its side. Keil and Delitzsch fix that bar at an equal distance from top and bottom, and Ellicott would render the phrase midway in the boards rather than in the midst of them. Gill notices the difficulty the wording leaves: it is said of the middle bar only that it reached from end to end, though one would expect as much of the others, and he supposes the rest may have come somewhat short.

The gilding raises a practical question the text ignores. Gill notes that the boards were not merely gilded but covered with thin plates of gold, and that because this would take a great quantity and make them heavy to carry, some have thought them only gilt after all. Clarke reaches the same place from the other end: how thick the gold was is not stated, and it was no doubt done with plates, but they must have been very thin or the boards would have been insupportably heavy — probably something like gold leaf, though not beaten so fine.

The section closes by referring everything back to what could not be written down. Ellicott's remark is the frankest: however minute the account has been — even tediously minute, he says — there must still have been a multitude of particulars that words could not convey, and for those Moses would have to be guided by the pattern he had seen. Keil and Delitzsch put the same thing as a limit on discretion rather than on language, since even the setting up and the position of the dwelling were prescribed and not left to human judgment. Gill simply places the command where it falls, when the work was finished and all its furniture complete.
31:
The purpose of the veil is stated first and agreed by everyone. Ellicott makes it of the essence of the dwelling that it should have an outer and an inner sanctuary — a place for the daily ministrations and an innermost chamber of extreme holiness where the divine presence was, which the high priest alone might enter, and he only once a year. Keil and Delitzsch give the word its sense of division and describe the curtain as woven in the same artistic manner as the inner covering of the walls, hung on four gilded pillars with golden hooks standing in silver sockets, so as to part the dwelling into two rooms of ten cubits and twenty.

What it signified draws four readings that do not quite coincide. Gill offers three in succession and settles on the last — the sin of man that separates God and man, removed when the veil was rent; or the obscurity of the legal dispensation, the gospel being veiled under the shadows of the law; or rather, he thinks, the human nature of Christ, the veil of his flesh. Clarke argues that from the root itself, which means to break or rend, and asks whether the Hebrew name does not intimate the typical correspondence with Christ's body, so that when that body was rent upon the cross the veil was rent also, from the top to the bottom. Calvin takes the obscurity as the principal thing: the veil told the Israelites that the time of full revelation had not yet come and that the spiritual worship of God was still enshrouded, so that their faith might stretch forward to the Messiah at whose coming the truth would be laid bare — and when Christ rose, the veil was rent and an end put to the ceremonies, because God then presented himself in his living and express image. Henry and Wesley take the same line from the Epistle to the Hebrews, that the way into the holiest was not made manifest while the first tabernacle stood, and add the practical consequence: we have boldness to enter now, yet a boldness that obliges us to reverence and a humble sense of our distance.

Calvin also notices what the arrangement did to the people rather than for them. Two veils together admonished them how reverently God's majesty must be regarded, so that they should not approach his presence without fear nor break boldly in upon sacred things.

On the fabric itself there is one small dispute. The Jews, Clarke reports, made the veil four fingers thick to prevent anyone seeing through it — and Calmet answers, as Clarke relays approvingly, that there was no necessity for any such thickness, since the tabernacle had no window and the simplest veil would have hidden whatever lay behind it, the only light being what came in at the door or from the candlestick standing outside the veil. Gill gives the same tradition without the objection, adding that the thread was six times doubled.
33:
Where exactly the veil hung is fixed by the clasps of the roof, and the consequence is disputed. Gill takes the point of meeting, where the two great pieces of tapestry were coupled, for the place of the partition, and cites Lightfoot: according to the division of the house was the division of the curtains, so that the veil parting the holy from the most holy hung just under the clasps. Keil and Delitzsch say the same and give the result in figures — the curtain divided the dwelling into two compartments, one of ten cubits and the other of twenty.

Ellicott is less willing to let the arithmetic follow so quickly. If under the taches means directly under them, he grants, we must regard the dwelling as divided into two chambers of equal size; but he thinks the preposition may be used with some vagueness, in which case the innermost chamber may here, as in the later Temple, have been only half the size of the outer one. He leaves the question there rather than deciding it, and the two readings sit against each other: a proportion the text seems to give and a proportion the later building actually had.

What went on either side of the curtain is set out without argument. Keil and Delitzsch have the ark of the testimony brought within, the mercy seat placed upon it, and the two remaining pieces of furniture set outside in the holy place, the candlestick opposite the table, the one on the south side and the other on the north. Gill adds the reading he takes from the arrangement. The mercy seat with the cherubim of glory overshadowing it he makes a representation of the way of man's salvation — flowing from the mercy of God, through the propitiation and the righteousness by which the law is fulfilled, and published in the gospel by its ministers, whom he sees signified in the cherubim. Of the two pieces left in the outer chamber he says only what their pairing suggests: that in the church, in its present state — of which the holy place was an emblem — there are both food and light.

The verse that names the division states plainly what the arrangement was for, and Keil and Delitzsch let it stand as the summary of the whole: the curtain was to divide for them between the holy place and the most holy. Everything in the chapter to this point — the two halves of the roof-cloth, the clasps that joined them, the four pillars and their silver sockets — exists to make and mark that one line, and Gill's placing of the ark and its mercy seat at the western end of the inner chamber is the last detail needed before the furniture of the outer one can be set in order.
36:
The last hanging is the one that faces the world, and Clarke orders the three coverings by their distance from it. This may be called the first veil, since it occupied the door; the curtain dividing the holy place from the most holy is the second; and these two, with the inner covering of the dwelling, were all of the same materials and the same workmanship.

Over what that workmanship was, Keil and Delitzsch part company with the rest — and with themselves. The hanging was of the same material as the inner curtain but of work in mixed colours, they say, not woven with figures upon it but simply in stripes or checks. The term does not mean coloured needlework with figures or flowers embroidered on a woven fabric, and they name the authorities they are contradicting, the Rabbins and Gesenius and Bähr among them, before adding that they had asserted the same thing themselves in an earlier book. Their grounds are lexical: in the only other place the word occurs it means to weave rather than to embroider, and the Arabic cognate means to make points, stripes or lines, to work in mixed colours. Since Ellicott had rested the whole distinction between the two kinds of work on precisely this word, the retraction unsettles more than one verse.

The five pillars raise a question of shape. Ellicott finds the odd number surprising beside the four of the interior, until one remembers that a tent of this kind must have a pillar in the middle of its gable end with an equal number of supports on either side — and it is this fifth pillar, together with the word used for the structure, that he says gives Fergusson's tent theory its solid basis. Gill accounts for the same five differently, one at each corner of the entrance and three spaced between, so as to leave four ways for the priests to go in, which the breadth easily allowed.

On the metals the commentators are exact and Gill is exact about the reason. The pillars were overlaid with plates rather than gilded, since a gild would soon wear off under continual passing and repassing; and the overlaying is to be understood not of the whole pillar but of the heads and their fillets, the wood showing in places. The sockets here were of brass — bronze, Ellicott would say — a meaner metal than the silver used for the veil's pillars, that being the entrance to the holy of holies and this only to the holy place.

Clarke closes the chapter by reversing its whole arrangement. In this tabernacle almost everything was placed out of the people's sight: the holiest inaccessible, the testimony comparatively hidden, the mercy seat and the divine glory with it. Under the gospel all these are laid open, the way into the holiest made manifest and the veil rent; the awful distance is abolished and the kingdom of heaven opened to all believers. What he asks of a reader struck by the costliness of the building is the corresponding thing — to consider how pure and holy that church must be of which all this was so expressive a type.
